A liquid boils at the temperature at which its vapour pressure becomes equal to the applied (atmospheric) pressure.

When a nonvolatile solute is dissolved in a solvent, the solute molecules occupy part of the surface, fewer solvent molecules escape per unit area, and the vapour pressure of the solution falls below that of the pure solvent at every temperature. Plotting vapour pressure against temperature (Fig. 2.6), the curve of the solution (CD) therefore lies BELOW that of the pure solvent (AB), and the gap widens as the temperature rises, since \(\Delta P = x_2P_1^0\) and \(P_1^0\) itself increases with temperature.

Because the solution's curve is lower, it crosses the 760 mm line further to the right. The solution must be heated to a higher temperature than the pure solvent before its vapour pressure reaches 1 atm. That extra heating is the boiling point elevation,

\(\Delta T_b = T_b - T_b^0\)

So boiling point elevation is a direct consequence of vapour pressure lowering: the more the vapour pressure is lowered, the more the boiling point rises.

Isotonic solutions : two or more solutions having the SAME osmotic pressure are said to be isotonic. For example 0.1 M urea and 0.1 M sucrose are isotonic, because both are nonelectrolytes at the same molarity and \(\pi = MRT\) is therefore the same for both. Such solutions have the same molar concentration but different concentrations in g/L, and if they are separated by a semipermeable membrane there is no net flow of solvent in either direction.

Hypertonic solution : of two solutions of unequal osmotic pressure, the more concentrated one, with the HIGHER osmotic pressure, is the hypertonic solution. The more dilute one, with the lower osmotic pressure, is hypotonic. For example, if the osmotic pressure of a sucrose solution is higher than that of a urea solution, the sucrose solution is hypertonic to the urea solution.

Yes. Solvent molecules pass through the semipermeable membrane in BOTH directions, because solvent is present on both sides of it — pure solvent on one side and solvent within the solution on the other.

What differs is the RATE. The vapour pressure (escaping tendency) of the pure solvent is greater than that of the solvent in the solution, so the rate at which solvent molecules pass from the solvent side into the solution is greater than the rate of the reverse passage. The result is a NET flow of solvent into the solution, and that net flow is what is called osmosis.

Osmosis is therefore not a one-way traffic but an inequality between two opposing flows; it stops when the two rates become equal, which is what the hydrostatic pressure eventually achieves.

Urea is a nonelectrolyte, so its osmotic pressure is the value \((\pi)_0\) expected for a nonelectrolyte at that concentration. Since both solutions have the SAME concentration and are at the SAME temperature, the van't Hoff factor follows directly from the ratio of the two measured pressures:

\(i = \dfrac{(\pi)}{(\pi)_0} = \dfrac{0.605\ \mathrm{atm}}{0.245\ \mathrm{atm}} = 2.47\)

The value is consistent with \(\mathrm{CaCl_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Ca^{2\oplus}} + 2\,\mathrm{Cl^{\ominus}}\), which would give \(i = 3\) on complete dissociation. The observed 2.47 is smaller because at this concentration electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions forms ion pairs, which reduces the number of independent particles in solution.

Osmosis is the flow of solvent through a semipermeable membrane INTO the solution. The direction of this flow can be reversed by applying to the solution a pressure LARGER than its osmotic pressure. The pure solvent then flows out of the solution, back through the membrane into the pure solvent compartment. This phenomenon is called reverse osmosis.

In the schematic set up (Fig. 2.10) fresh water and salt water are separated by a semipermeable membrane. When a pressure greater than the osmotic pressure of the salt water is applied to it with a piston, pure water is forced out of the salty water through the membrane into the fresh water compartment, from which it is drawn off at the water outlet.

Reverse osmosis is therefore the basis of the desalination of sea water and of domestic water purifiers.

For a dilute solution the osmotic pressure is

\(\pi = \dfrac{n_2RT}{V}\)

where \(n_2\) is the number of moles of solute in volume \(V\) (in \(\mathrm{dm^3}\)) of solution.

If \(\mathrm{W_2}\) g of solute of molar mass \(M_2\) is dissolved, then \(n_2 = \mathrm{W_2}/M_2\), and substitution gives

\(\pi = \dfrac{\mathrm{W_2}RT}{M_2V}\) or \(M_2 = \dfrac{\mathrm{W_2}RT}{\pi V}\)

So a known mass \(\mathrm{W_2}\) of the substance is dissolved to make a known volume \(V\) of solution, the osmotic pressure \(\pi\) of that solution is measured at a known temperature \(T\), and the molar mass is obtained from the equation above. Because osmotic pressure is large and precisely measurable, only a small mass of solute is required.

The vapour pressure of a liquid depends on the ease with which its molecules escape from the SURFACE of the liquid.

When a nonvolatile solute is dissolved in the solvent, some of the solvent molecules at the surface are replaced by solute molecules. Being nonvolatile, those solute molecules contribute nothing to the vapour above the solution. Hence the number of solvent molecules available for vaporization per unit surface area of the solution is smaller than the number at the surface of the pure solvent.

As a result the solvent molecules at the surface of the solution vaporize at a slower rate than those of the pure solvent, and the equilibrium vapour pressure established above the solution is lower. This is the lowering of vapour pressure, \(\Delta P = P_1^0 - P_1\).

Raoult's law for a solution of a nonvolatile solute states

\(P_1 = P_1^0x_1\)

where \(x_1\) is the mole fraction of the solvent.

For a binary solution containing one solute, the two mole fractions add to unity:

\(x_1 = 1 - x_2\)

Substituting,

\(P_1 = P_1^0(1 - x_2) = P_1^0 - P_1^0x_2\)

Rearranging,

\(P_1^0 - P_1 = P_1^0x_2\)

The left-hand side is by definition the lowering of vapour pressure, \(\Delta P = P_1^0 - P_1\). Hence

\(\Delta P = P_1^0x_2\)

Since \(P_1^0\) is a constant at a given temperature, this shows that \(\Delta P\) depends only on \(x_2\), that is, only on the number of solute particles — which is why the lowering of vapour pressure is a colligative property.

Because in these two measurements the temperature is NOT constant — the whole point of the experiment is to measure a change of temperature, \(\Delta T_b\) or \(\Delta T_f\).

Molarity is moles of solute per \(\mathrm{dm^3}\) of SOLUTION, and the volume of a solution expands or contracts as the temperature changes, so molarity changes with temperature. Molality is moles of solute per kilogram of SOLVENT; both quantities are masses, and mass does not change with temperature, so molality is temperature independent.

Expressing the concentration in molality therefore keeps the concentration fixed while the temperature is varied, and \(\Delta T_b = K_b m\) and \(\Delta T_f = K_f m\) remain valid throughout the measurement. Osmotic pressure is the exception, being measured at one constant temperature, and there molarity is used.
